introduction-can-you-trust-your-own-os.core: Software can't fully vouch for itself: a rootkit in the bootloader or kernel can make every security tool report 'all clear'. Trust must start from something immutable, a hardware root of trust, and extend step by step: each boot stage verifies or measures the next before running it. Attestation then lets the machine prove to a remote party, cryptographically, exactly what booted, so secrets are released only to healthy systems.

first_principles.problem: A bootkit loads before the OS, hides from antivirus, and persists through reinstalls.
truths: Each stage must check the next.

analogy.title: Checking a witness's credibility through who vouches for them
analogy.story: You trust A because B vouches, B because C does, and so on, back to someone whose integrity is beyond question.
analogy.breaks: Witnesses can be bribed later; measurements are recorded at load time and can't be undone.

example.title: Why self-checks fail
flow: Need: measurement taken before bootkit could act

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Shows why trust must come from below the OS.

check.q: Why can't antivirus reliably detect a bootkit?
check.a: It runs on an OS the bootkit already controls, so the OS can hide the bootkit from it.

the-chain-of-trust-secure-boot-vs-measur.core: Secure Boot and Measured Boot are complementary. Secure Boot enforces: UEFI firmware checks each bootloader and kernel signature against trusted keys (db/dbx) and refuses to run unsigned code. Measured Boot records: each stage hashes the next and extends the hash into TPM PCRs before running it, creating a tamper-evident log of what actually booted, even if it was allowed. Secure Boot blocks known-bad code; Measured Boot lets a remote verifier decide.

first_principles.problem: Secure Boot is on, but a signed yet vulnerable bootloader (BootHole) is loaded and exploited, and nothing records it.

analogy.title: A bouncer versus a guest book
analogy.story: The bouncer refuses anyone not on the list; the guest book records everyone who came in, so you can review it later.
analogy.breaks: A guest book can be forged; PCRs can only be extended, never rewritten.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: You can see what was enforced and what was measured.

code.text:
mokutil --sb-state                 # SecureBoot enabled
tpm2_pcrread sha256:0,4,7          # firmware, bootloader, SB policy
tpm2_eventlog /sys/kernel/security/tpm0/binary_bios_measurements | head

check.q: Why is Measured Boot useful even with Secure Boot enabled?
check.a: It records exactly what ran, including signed-but-vulnerable code, so a verifier can reject it.

the-hardware-ledger-trusted-platform-mod.core: A TPM is a small secure cryptoprocessor (a discrete chip, firmware, or virtual vTPM) holding keys that never leave it and Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs). PCRs can only be extended (new = hash(old || measurement)), never set, so their final value summarises everything measured since reset. The TPM can sign PCR values with an attestation key (a quote), seal data to PCR states, and store keys bound to the device via its unique Endorsement Key.

first_principles.problem: A server needs to prove its boot state and store a disk key that only works if boot hasn't changed.
truths: Keys in hardware can't be copied.
Device identity needs a unique key.

analogy.title: A ledger written in permanent ink where each line includes a summary of all lines before
analogy.story: You can add lines but never erase, and the last line proves the whole history.
analogy.breaks: A ledger is readable; TPM keys inside are not.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One value captures the whole boot sequence.

code.text:
import hashlib
pcr = bytes(32)                               # reset value
for stage in [b"firmware", b"grub", b"vmlinuz"]:
    m = hashlib.sha256(stage).digest()
    pcr = hashlib.sha256(pcr + m).digest()   # extend
print(pcr.hex())   # changes if any stage or the order changes

check.q: Why can't malware just set a PCR to the expected value?
check.a: PCRs can only be extended by hashing; reaching a specific value would require breaking SHA-256.

releasing-secrets-sealing-and-unsealing.core: Sealing encrypts data with a TPM key under a policy, typically that specific PCRs hold expected values. Unseal succeeds only when the machine is in that measured state. BitLocker and systemd-cryptenroll use this to unlock disks automatically on a trusted boot: if someone boots a different OS, changes the bootloader or moves the disk to another machine, the TPM refuses and recovery is required. Policies can add PINs and must handle legitimate updates.

first_principles.problem: A stolen laptop's disk is booted from USB to read files, or the disk is moved to another machine.
truths: Keys should depend on platform state.
The TPM enforces policy in hardware.
derivation: Use **signed PCR policies** to survive updates.

analogy.title: A safe that only opens in your own house, with the lights arranged a certain way
analogy.story: Move it, or change the room, and it stays shut.
analogy.breaks: Rearranging furniture yourself (OS updates) also locks it, unless the policy anticipates it.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The disk only unlocks on its own trusted boot.

code.text:
systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=auto --tpm2-pcrs=7+11 /dev/nvme0n1p3
# /etc/crypttab: root /dev/nvme0n1p3 - tpm2-device=auto
# boot from USB → PCR 7/11 differ → TPM refuses → recovery key needed

check.q: Why do firmware updates often trigger BitLocker recovery?
check.a: Measurements change, so the PCR policy no longer matches unless it's resealed or uses signed policies.

remote-attestation-proving-health-to-the.core: Remote attestation lets a verifier check a device's state over the network. The verifier sends a fresh nonce, and the device's TPM returns a quote: selected PCR values plus the nonce, signed by an attestation key certified as belonging to a genuine TPM (via the EK certificate). The verifier replays the event log to confirm it matches the PCRs and compares against known-good values, then issues credentials or access. The nonce prevents replaying an old healthy quote.

first_principles.problem: A zero-trust network wants to grant production access only to laptops and servers with a verified, unmodified boot chain.
truths: The verifier must trust the signer is a real TPM.

analogy.title: A health certificate signed by a trusted doctor, dated today
analogy.story: The border agent checks the doctor's licence, today's date and the results before letting you through.
analogy.breaks: Doctors examine you live; attestation proves boot-time state, not current runtime state.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Access depends on proven boot integrity.

code.text:
# verifier: NONCE=$(openssl rand -hex 16)
tpm2_quote -c ak.ctx -l sha256:0,4,7 -q $NONCE -m quote.msg -s quote.sig -o pcrs.bin
# verifier:
tpm2_checkquote -u ak.pub -m quote.msg -s quote.sig -f pcrs.bin -q $NONCE

check.q: What attack does the nonce prevent?
check.a: Replay: re-sending an old quote captured when the device was still healthy.

the-ima-subsystem-extending-attestation-.core: Boot measurements stop at the kernel. Linux IMA (Integrity Measurement Architecture) extends measurement into runtime: it hashes executables, libraries and config files when they're opened or run, logs them, and extends PCR 10. Remote verifiers (such as Keylime) can check the IMA log against an allow-list to detect unexpected binaries. In appraisal mode, IMA/EVM enforce that files carry valid signatures and refuse to execute modified ones.

first_principles.problem: A server boots cleanly, but an attacker later drops a modified sshd binary that boot attestation never sees.
truths: Files can be measured at use.
Logs must be bounded by policy.
derivation: Tune the **policy** to control log volume.

analogy.title: A building that logs every badge swipe after opening, not just the morning lock-up check
analogy.story: You know who entered which room all day, not only that the doors were locked at dawn.
analogy.breaks: Logging everything is noisy; IMA policies must choose what to measure.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The tampered sshd is detected at runtime.

code.text:
# kernel cmdline: ima_policy=tcb ima_hash=sha256
head -3 /sys/kernel/security/ima/ascii_runtime_measurements
# 10 <hash> ima-ng sha256:<filehash> /usr/sbin/sshd
# Keylime verifier alerts if sshd's hash isn't on the allow-list

check.q: What does IMA appraisal add over measurement?
check.a: Enforcement: files without valid hashes or signatures are blocked, not just logged.
